newsitem.title: USA: Netanyahu to pay US hospital visit to King Hussein.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu to pay US hospital visit to King Hussein.

text.p: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, preparing for new crisis talks on the stalled Middle East peace process, headed to a Minnesota hospital on Sunday for discussions with a convalescing King Hussein of Jordan.

The prime minister was scheduled to be in this medical centre city for only about five hours before leaving for Washington and a crucial meeting on Monday with President Bill Clinton. His hospital room visit with the monarch would likely last only a short time.

But the "Mayo Clinic mini-summit," as local press dubbed the meeting at the renowned medical facility where Hussein was recovering from prostate surgery, could give the Israeli leader more backing for proposed quick-pace negotiations to reach a comprehensive settlement over six months.

Jordan believes Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat would be wise to take Netanyahu up on his offer of rapid go-for-broke talks -- provided the Palestinians can get a clear picture from Israel on what the talks would encompass.
But Netanyahu showed no signs of backing away from the latest flashpoint in the crisis -- a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem that has unleashed Palestinian rage.
"The construction in Jerusalem, the construction on Har Homa, will continue," the prime minister's cabinet secretary Danny Naveh told Israel army radio before the party flew to the United States.
Clashes have erupted nearly every day since Israel broke ground last month on Har Homa, a 6,500-home project on a hilltop that Palestinians call Jabal Abu Ghneim and on land each side claims.

Arafat was enroute to India to urge Non-Aligned Movement nations "to support Palestinian political rights and condemn the Israeli settlement activity," his adviser, Nabil Abu Rdainah, told Reuters on Sunday.
Palestinian cabinet minister Hanan Ashrawi was due in Washington to present Arafat's views to U.S. officials on the settlements and the future of Jerusalem.

The Palestinians have said Arafat will not negotiate with Netanyahu unless work stops on the new settlement. Israel meanwhile, has accused Arafat of giving a green light to suicide bombings and said a crackdown against "terrorism" is a condition for future talks.
The Palestinian Centre for Public Opinion said on Sunday that 48.6 percent of 470 Palestinians polled backed suicide attacks against Israel as support sinks for peace talks with the Jewish state.

U.S. officials said they had ideas for breaking the deadlock that would be put to Netanyahu and, by telephone, to Arafat. "We are developing our own ideas and we're going to put them forward," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
Netanyahu was expected to come under heavy pressure from Washington to at least make a gesture to revive the peace process that has been stalled for about a month.

But on the eve of the Netanyahu-Clinton meeting, Israel's ambassador to Washington, Eliahu Ben-Elissar, said his country was feeling no U.S. pressure, telling Israel Radio: "There's nary a sign of it. To tell you the truth, I also don't believe there will be a pressure campaign."

Israeli officials have said the Clinton administration shares Israel's view that the root of the crisis was not settlements but the Palestinians' use of violence and "terrorism" as a political bargaining chip.

Netanyahu hopes to get Clinton behind his offer to seal a final peace within six months -- instead of the original 1999 deadline -- ending if necessary, with an intensive U.S.- Israeli-Palestinian summit akin to the 1978 Camp David meeting that paved the way to Israeli-Egyptian peace.

The 61-year-old Hussein was reported resting comfortably at Mayo's Methodist Hospital following routine surgery on Saturday in which a benign enlargement of his prostate was removed. Doctors said they found no sign of cancer that was removed during surgery at the same facility in 1962.
He will likely be released from the hospital this week.
Israel claims all of Jerusalem as its capital. The Palestinians want East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in 1967 along with the rest of the West Bank, as capital of a future state.

Palestinians see new Jewish settlements as an effort to pre-empt the negotiations they are supposed to hold on the future of East Jerusalem and the rest the West Bank and Gaza under agreements signed by the previous Israeli government.
